questions.q: What term is used to describe the fundamental building blocks that make up all matter around us?
questions.a: The fundamental building blocks of matter are called constituent particles, which include atoms, molecules, or ions. A wrong answer like "cells" or "atoms only" shows confusion between biological units of life and chemical units of matter, or ignores that compounds are made of molecules.

questions.q: When a solid dissolves in a liquid, why does the volume of the liquid not increase significantly, even though matter has been added?
questions.a: The volume does not increase significantly because the constituent particles of liquids have spaces between them (inter-particle space), into which the smaller particles of the dissolved solid fit. A wrong answer stating that "the solid vanishes into nothing" shows a misconception that matter can be destroyed rather than understanding particle spacing.

questions.q: If you have a pure sample of copper wire and a pure sample of water, what are the primary constituent particles that make up each of these substances respectively?
questions.a: Copper is an element made of individual copper atoms, while water is a compound made of water molecules ($H_2O$). To find this, we recognize that metals exist primarily as discrete atoms, whereas non-metal combinations form molecules. A wrong answer stating both are made of molecules indicates a failure to distinguish between elemental substances and molecular compounds.

questions.q: Analyze a sample of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) gas and a sample of oxygen ($O_2$) gas. How do their constituent particles compare in terms of composition?
questions.a: Both are made of molecules, but an oxygen molecule ($O_2$) consists of two atoms of the same element (oxygen), whereas a carbon dioxide molecule ($CO_2$) consists of one carbon atom chemically bonded to two oxygen atoms. A wrong answer claiming they are identical because both are gases shows a failure to look at microscopic chemical composition.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The constituent particles of a solid are completely stationary and locked in a fixed position, so they possess no energy whatsoever." Is this scientifically accurate? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: This statement is inaccurate. While the constituent particles of a solid are tightly packed and cannot move from place to place, they still vibrate constantly about their fixed mean positions because they possess vibrational kinetic energy. A wrong answer accepting the statement as true reveals a misconception that lack of macroscopic movement equals absolute stillness at the microscopic particle level.

questions.q: Design a simple mental model or physical analogy using everyday Indian household items (such as marbles, grains of dal, or puffed rice) to demonstrate how constituent particles are arranged differently in a solid versus a gas.
questions.a: A good response would describe tightly packing identical marbles in a box so they touch and cannot move easily to represent a solid, and scattering a few puffed rice grains far apart in a large container with plenty of empty space to represent a gas. A poor response would use inconsistent objects or fail to represent the spatial arrangement and spacing differences between states of matter.
